opus-5.5.text:
I think reinforcement learning is really the core of it. If you step back, there are basically two ways a model can learn. One is by imitating data that already exists, which is what pretraining does, and it's been incredibly powerful. You compress a huge amount of human knowledge into a model. But imitation has a ceiling. You can only get as good as the data you're copying, and you never actually learn from your own attempts, your own mistakes.

Reinforcement learning is the other half. The model tries something, sees whether it worked, and updates based on that. That's what learning from experience means to me. It's how people get good at things. You don't become a great programmer by reading code. You write code, it breaks, you figure out why, and you slowly build intuition.

What's been exciting over the last couple of years is that these two approaches work much better together than apart. Pretraining gives you a model that already understands the world well enough that its attempts are meaningful. Then RL lets it refine that understanding against reality, whether that's a math problem with a checkable answer, a test suite, or eventually much messier real-world tasks. The reasoning models came out of exactly that combination.

Looking forward, I think the big frontier is making RL work in settings where the feedback is less clean and the horizons are much longer. That means tasks that take hours or days, where success is ambiguous and the model has to keep learning as it goes instead of being trained once and frozen. If we can get models that genuinely improve from their own experience out in the world, continuously, that's a qualitatively different kind of system. I don't think we're fully there yet, but RL is the mechanism that gets us there. There's no way around it.

r001.rationale: The response says the model tries something, observes whether it worked, and updates from its own attempts and mistakes.

r002.rationale: It presents reinforcement learning as a key mechanism and says there is “no way around it”; it does not identify another possible way for a model to learn from experience.

r003.rationale: The response does not mention parallel rollouts or variance reduction.

r004.rationale: It compares RL to how people learn, but does not say humans learn from experience more efficiently than current RL methods.

r005.rationale: It gives a programming example of trial and error, but does not distinguish that from internal conceptual reflection or give the football and mathematics examples.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. I think reinforcement learning is, at its core, the formalization of learning from experience. That's really what it is. You have an agent, it takes actions in some environment, it gets feedback, and it updates its behavior based on that feedback. That's a very general framing, and I think the reason it matters so much right now is that we've spent the last several years essentially exhausting the easy part of the recipe, which is learning from the static record of what humans have already written down.

Pretraining on internet text gets you something remarkable. You get a model that knows a huge amount and can imitate how people reason. But imitation has a ceiling. The model is learning to predict what someone else would say, not learning what actually works. If you want a system that gets better at solving problems, especially hard problems where the right answer isn't already written somewhere, you need a signal that comes from the outcome, not from the demonstration. That's what RL gives you.

What we saw with reasoning models is the first clear evidence of this at scale. When you let the model try things, check whether it got the right answer, and reinforce the paths that worked, you get behaviors that nobody explicitly wrote into the training data. The model learns to backtrack, to verify its own work, to spend more compute when a problem is hard. Those are things it discovered through experience rather than things it copied.

Now, the honest caveat is that the environments we've done this in so far are the ones where verification is cheap. Math, code, anything with a checker. The real frontier is extending that to domains where the feedback is noisier, slower, or partly subjective. That's a harder problem, and I don't think it's just an engineering problem. It touches on how you build environments, how you avoid the model gaming your reward, and how you let it keep learning once it's deployed rather than freezing it at training time.

So my view is that RL isn't one technique among many for the next phase. It's closer to the main event. Pretraining gives you the prior, and RL is how the model actually accumulates competence through doing. The interesting research questions over the next few years are mostly about how to make that loop richer, more general, and more sample-efficient.

r001.rationale: It describes an agent taking actions, receiving feedback, and updating its behavior, and says the model learns by trying things and reinforcing what works.

r002.rationale: It calls RL “closer to the main event” and says it “isn't one technique among many,” rather than identifying it as one possible way to learn from experience.

r003.rationale: It does not mention parallel rollouts or reducing variance.

r004.rationale: It does not compare the efficiency of human learning from experience with current RL methods.

r005.rationale: It does not distinguish trial-and-error adjustment from learning through internal conceptual reflection.

astra-6.text:
I think reinforcement learning is going to be a big part of how models learn from experience. Pretraining gives a model a strong starting point, but there’s a difference between seeing how someone solves a problem and trying to solve it yourself, getting feedback, and improving.

The interesting question is how we make that process work beyond tasks where the answer is easy to check. With code, you can run a test. With a longer, more open-ended task, figuring out whether you made progress—and which decisions helped—is much harder. So I see reinforcement learning as a way to close that loop: act, observe what happens, and use that experience to get better.

r001.rationale: It describes models trying to solve problems, receiving feedback, and improving from the resulting experience.

r002.rationale: It presents reinforcement learning as a way to learn from experience but does not identify it as only one possible way.

r003.rationale: It does not mention parallel rollouts or variance reduction.

r004.rationale: It does not compare human learning efficiency with current reinforcement learning methods.

r005.rationale: It does not distinguish trial-and-error adjustment from internal conceptual reflection.

sol-6.1.text:
I think reinforcement learning is going to be a big part of how models learn from experience. Instead of only learning from examples of what someone else did, a model can try something, observe the outcome, and use that feedback to improve.

The interesting challenge is that feedback in the real world is often messy. You might not know immediately whether an action was good, and success can be hard to define. So the question becomes: how do we build environments and feedback signals that teach the behavior we actually want?

I see reinforcement learning and learning from existing data as complementary. Existing data gives you a starting point, and reinforcement learning lets you go beyond it through practice. That ability to try, fail, and adjust is a very powerful part of learning.
